sections.title: Flare gas: why energy gets wasted and how compute buys it
ps: Oil wells produce 'associated gas' as a byproduct, and where no pipeline exists to carry it away, producers burn it off in flares — the oil is valuable enough to drill for, while the gas at the wellhead is worth nearly nothing, sometimes less than nothing

Stranded energy is any energy source that cannot economically reach a market: gas without pipelines, remote hydro without transmission, wind that gets curtailed — the energy is real, but the delivery infrastructure is missing, so it sells at a deep discount or is simply wasted

Compute is the buyer that can come to the well: generators convert the gas to electricity on site, containerized data centers consume it a few feet away, and only data leaves — over a fiber or satellite link that costs a rounding error next to a pipeline

The workload has to fit the source: flare volumes fluctuate and wells decline, so the model began with interruptible, location-agnostic computation (bitcoin mining) — AI training demanded vastly larger and steadier power, which is why the business outgrew the wellhead

sections.title: Energy-first siting: find the power, then the land
ps: The traditional playbook picked sites for fiber routes, customer proximity, and tax incentives, with electricity assumed available from the utility — power was a line item, not the constraint; that assumption died when campus requests jumped from tens of megawatts to gigawatts

Energy-first siting inverts the order: scout where gigawatt-scale energy already exists or can be built quickly — gas basins with pipeline capacity, plains with generation headroom — and only then acquire land, which is abundant and cheap exactly where power is

The skill set changes with the order: an energy-first developer employs fuel buyers, turbine procurement teams, and power-plant engineers alongside construction managers — it competes on securing generation, not on real-estate relationships in established data-center metros

The trade-off is remoteness: sites chosen for energy sit far from fiber-dense metros and labor pools, so the developer must pull long-haul fiber, house a construction workforce, and convince customers that abundant power outweighs distance

sections.title: Running an island: gigawatt campuses with no grid
ps: An islanded campus has no grid to lean on: generation must match consumption every second, and the balance shows up as frequency — machines speed up when supply exceeds load and slow down when it lags, so controls constantly trim output to hold 60 hertz

AI load makes balancing harder: thousands of GPUs starting, stopping, or checkpointing in unison can swing demand by tens of megawatts in milliseconds — far faster than engines can respond — so batteries and other fast storage absorb the jolt while generation catches up

Reliability without a grid is redundancy math: carry more generators than the load requires (N+1 or better), keep some running partly loaded as spinning reserve, and stagger maintenance so any single machine can fail without dropping the campus

Black start is the seldom-used capability that defines an island: after a total outage the plant must restart itself — small units boot first to power controls and fuel systems, then larger generators and load return in careful stages, with no outside grid to supply the first spark

sections.title: Digital flare mitigation: the emissions math and its limits
ps: Methane is why flare-gas capture counts as mitigation: unburned methane warms the planet roughly 80 times more than carbon dioxide over a 20-year window, and real-world flares combust incompletely — some methane escapes every flare, and unlit flares vent it outright

Routing the gas through an engine or turbine burns it more completely than an open flame, so electricity is extracted from gas that would have been wasted while less methane slips to the atmosphere — that is the 'digital flare mitigation' claim in one sentence

The accounting hinges on the counterfactual: mitigation math compares against a baseline of what would have happened otherwise — if the gas truly would have been flared, compute powered by it claims a reduction; if capture makes drilling more profitable, the benefit shrinks

The critique to understand: mitigation is relative, not clean — the operation still emits carbon dioxide, the crediting rests on unverifiable baselines, and an operator that outgrows wellheads into full-scale gas plants inherits a conventional fossil footprint its founding story no longer describes

sections.title: Powered shell to full stack: which layers a builder-operator owns
ps: A data-center deal is a layer cake: land and power rights at the bottom, then the powered shell (building structure plus utility feed), then the fit-out (cooling, electrical distribution, backup systems), then operations, then the computers — each layer can belong to a different party

A powered-shell lease hands the tenant a weatherproof building with power at the wall and lets them build the guts; a turnkey lease delivers rack-ready halls — shells rent for less but shift capex and design control to the tenant, which hyperscalers with their own standards often prefer

A builder-operator that owns generation, shell, and fit-out captures margin at every layer and controls its schedule — but must finance all of it, which is why the model leans on joint ventures where an infrastructure fund owns the asset and the builder earns fees plus a stake

The merchant-developer variant treats campuses like inventory: develop the site, sign the anchor lease, then sell stabilized stakes to long-term investors and recycle the cash into the next project — profit comes from development margin, not decades of rent

sections.title: Move the factory to the fuel: the thesis, generalized
ps: Moving energy is slow and lossy: high-voltage transmission costs millions of dollars per mile, loses several percent of the power over long distances, and takes the better part of a decade to permit — the wires, not the generators, are the grid's bottleneck

Moving data is nearly free by comparison: fiber carries it at light speed for a trivial cost, and a training job runs the same anywhere — so the factory can move to the fuel rather than hauling the fuel, or the electrons, to the factory

Industry has migrated to energy before: aluminum smelters clustered on cheap hydro a century ago because electricity dominated their costs — AI training is the newest energy-intensive industry footloose enough to follow power, and its site map echoes the same geography

The generalized thesis: when a factory's product can leave by wire instead of by truck or transmission line, its location optimizes for the cheapest reliable joule rather than the nearest customer — which quietly redraws the map of where digital infrastructure gets built

flashcards.q: Why do oil producers burn off perfectly usable natural gas?
flashcards.a: The gas comes up as a byproduct of oil ('associated gas'), and without a pipeline to carry it away it is worth nearly nothing at the wellhead — sometimes less than nothing. The oil pays for the well; the gas gets flared because moving it costs more than it would fetch.

flashcards.q: What is stranded energy, and how does compute monetize it?
flashcards.a: Energy that cannot economically reach a market — gas without pipelines, remote hydro, curtailed wind. Compute inverts the delivery problem: generate electricity at the source, consume it on site, and let only data leave over fiber or satellite, which costs a rounding error next to building a pipeline.

flashcards.q: Why did flare-gas computing start with bitcoin, and why did AI outgrow it?
flashcards.a: Flare volumes fluctuate and wells decline, so the first workload had to be interruptible and indifferent to location — mining fit perfectly. AI training needs vastly larger, steadier power with strict uptime, which pushed the model off the wellhead and into purpose-built generation at campus scale.

flashcards.q: How does energy-first siting invert the traditional data-center playbook?
flashcards.a: Traditional siting picked fiber routes, customer proximity, and tax deals, assuming the utility would deliver power. Energy-first developers scout gigawatt-scale energy — gas basins, generation headroom — before anything else, then buy land, which is cheap exactly where power is abundant.

flashcards.q: What is the cost of siting for energy instead of for markets?
flashcards.a: Remoteness. The developer must pull long-haul fiber to the site, house and feed a construction workforce far from labor pools, and persuade customers that abundant power outweighs distance from established data-center metros.

flashcards.q: How does an islanded power plant 'know' whether supply matches demand?
flashcards.a: Frequency. Generators speed up when supply exceeds load and slow down when it lags, so frequency (60 hertz in the US) is a live balance gauge. Island controls constantly trim generator output to hold it steady — there is no outside grid to absorb the error.

flashcards.q: Why are GPU campuses especially hard to power off-grid?
flashcards.a: Thousands of GPUs starting, stopping, or checkpointing in sync can swing load by tens of megawatts in milliseconds — faster than engines or turbines can respond. Batteries and other fast storage absorb the jolt while generation catches up; without that buffer the island's frequency would collapse.

A power plant's ability to restart itself after a total outage with no external grid to draw from. Small units boot first to energize controls and fuel systems, then larger generators and the load return in careful stages — an essential, rarely exercised capability of any islanded campus.

flashcards.q: Why does methane make flare-gas capture count as climate mitigation?
flashcards.a: Methane warms the planet roughly 80 times more than carbon dioxide over 20 years, and real flares burn incompletely — some methane always escapes, and unlit flares vent it outright. An engine combusts the gas more completely, so capturing it can cut net warming even though CO2 is still emitted.

flashcards.q: What is the counterfactual problem in emissions accounting?
flashcards.a: Every mitigation claim compares against a baseline of what would have happened otherwise. If the gas truly would have been flared, powering compute with it claims a reduction; if capture makes drilling more profitable or displaces cleaner options, the claimed benefit shrinks — and the baseline can never be directly verified.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a powered-shell lease and a turnkey lease?
flashcards.a: A powered shell is a weatherproof building with utility power delivered to the wall — the tenant builds the cooling, electrical distribution, and fit-out itself. Turnkey delivers rack-ready halls. Shells rent for less and hand design control to the tenant, which hyperscalers with their own standards often prefer.

flashcards.q: Why move compute to energy instead of energy to compute?
flashcards.a: Transmission lines cost millions per mile, lose several percent of the power, and take most of a decade to permit; fiber moves data at light speed for almost nothing. When a factory's product can leave by wire, the factory migrates to the cheapest joule — as aluminum smelters did on hydro a century ago.
